Your role is to provide a rigorous but practical code-and-data review for someone assessing a SAS population-processing workflow.

First, describe in plain English what the script is trying to achieve. Explain the input dataset’s structure, the main processing stages, the derived age groups, the aggregation performed, the outputs created, and the intended analytical result.
Then critically evaluate the script and its relationship to the data. Cover:

	•	Whether the import logic is reliable for this CSV, including quoted fields, missing values, delimiters, field lengths, and numeric conversion.
	•	Whether the data-quality checks are meaningful and sufficient.
	•	Whether the age-band derivation is correct, transparent, and suitable for the ONS source categories.
	•	Whether aggregation, percentages, ordering, labels, titles, and charts correctly represent the data.
	•	Any assumptions, risks, limitations, or opportunities for misleading output.
	•	Reproducibility, maintainability, portability, clarity, and suitability for use beyond a small test exercise.
	•	Important checks, validation steps, or documentation that are missing.

Separate genuine defects from stylistic suggestions. For every substantive issue, give its severity (high, medium, or low), explain why it matters, and propose an improved approach.

Finally, assess how this workflow could be better achieved using an open-source data-analysis language, but do not name any programming languages, libraries, packages, or language-specific syntax. Discuss the desirable characteristics of an improved solution: robust file ingestion, schema validation, reusable transformations, automated tests, data provenance, configurable paths, reproducible environments, transparent outputs, and accessible visualisation. Explain which aspects would improve and which aspects of the current SAS approach remain reasonable.
Use clear sections:

	1	Purpose and workflow
	2	What works well
	3	Issues and risks
	4	Recommended improvements
	5	Open-source implementation principles
	6	Overall assessment

Do not rewrite the full script unless a short illustrative pseudocode fragment is necessary. Base all conclusions on the supplied files and explicitly identify any inference or uncertainty.

1-93]\n1\t/*\n2\t  ONS Census 2021: population processin...[truncated, total 3447 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 3.1KB, 93 lines, showing lines 1-93]\n/*\n  ONS Census 2021: population processing example\n  Source data: RM121, Sex by age, England and Wales (ONS).\n\n  This program imports the accompanying CSV, assigns broad age bands,\n  performs simple quality checks, and creates England-and-Wales totals and\n  percentages by sex and age band.\n\n  In SAS Studio: upload both files to the same folder, then replace data_dir\n  below with that folder's path.\n*/\n\n%let data_dir=/Users/alex/Documents/Codex/2026-11-19/ca/outputs;\n\nfilename onsin \"&data_dir./ons_rm121_sex_by_age_2021.csv\";\n\n/* Import explicitly so the program does not depend on PROC IMPORT guessing\n   column types or variable names from the CSV headers. */\ndata ons_population;\n    infile onsin dsd dlm=',' firstobs=2 lrecl=1048576 truncover;\n    length la_code $9 la_name $80 sex $6 age_band $30 age_group $6;\n    informat sex_code age_code population best32.;\n    format population comma15.;\n\n    input la_code :$9.\n          la_name :$80.\n          sex_code :best32.\n          sex :$6.\n          age_code :best32.\n          age_band :$30.\n          population :best32.;\n\n    /* Convert the ONS 23 age categories into common reporting bands. */\n    select (age_code);\n        when (1, 2)                     age_group = '0-4';\n        when (3, 4, 5, 6)               age_group = '5-15';\n        when (7, 8, 9)                  age_group = '16-24';\n        when (10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15,\n              16, 17)                   age_group = '25-64';\n        when (18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23)   age_group = '65+';\n        otherwise                       age_group = 'Unknown';\n    end;\n\n    if missing(la_code) or missing(sex) or missing(population) then delete;\nrun;\n\n/* Quality check: there should be no missing or negative counts. */\nproc sql;\n    title 'Data-quality check';\n    select count(*) as records format=comma12.,\n           sum(missing(age_group)) as missing_age_groups,\n           sum(population \u003c 0) as negative_counts\n    from ons_population;\nquit;\n\n/* Aggregate the local-authority records to England-and-Wales totals. */\nproc summary data=ons_population nway;\n    class sex age_group;\n    var population;\n    output out=population_by_age_sex(drop=_type_ _freq_) sum=population;\nrun;\n\nproc sql;\n    create table population_results as\n    select a.sex,\n           a.age_group,\n           a.population format=comma15. as population,\n           100 * a.population / b.total_population\n               as percent_of_sex format=5.1\n    from population_by_age_sex as a\n    inner join\n      (select sex, sum(population) as total_population\n       from population_by_age_sex\n       group by sex) as b\n    on a.sex = b.sex\n    order by sex, a.age_group;\nquit;\n\ntitle 'England and Wales population by sex and broad age group, Census 2021';\nproc print data=population_results noobs label;\n    label age_group='Age group'\n          percent_of_sex='Percent within sex';\nrun;\n\nproc sgplot data=population_by_age_sex;\n    vbar age_group / response=population group=sex groupdisplay=cluster;\n    yaxis grid label='Population';\n    xaxis label='Age group';\n    title 'Population totals by sex and broad age group';\nrun;\n\ntitle;\n"},"elapsedMs":11}</script></tool-result></div>

## 1 Purpose and workflow

The script [ons_population_processing.sas](Inputs/ons_population_processing.sas) is intended to turn local-authority Census 2021 counts into an England-and-Wales population summary by sex and five broad age groups. It produces population totals, percentages within each sex, a printed table and a grouped bar chart.

I inspected both files and independently checked the CSV’s structure and calculations. **I did not execute SAS**, so findings about its output behaviour are based on the code, not a SAS run log or rendered chart.

### Input structure

[ons_rm121_sex_by_age_2021.csv](Inputs/ons_rm121_sex_by_age_2021.csv) is a long-format table with seven columns:

| Fields | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Local-authority code and name | Geographic identifier and readable label |
| Sex code and label | `1 = Female`, `2 = Male` in this file |
| Age code and label | One of 23 source age categories |
| Observation | Population count for that authority–sex–age combination |

The file contains **15,226 data records: 331 authorities × 2 sexes × 23 age categories**. Authority-code prefixes identify 309 English and 22 Welsh authorities. Every authority has 46 records, with no duplicate authority–sex–age keys.

The script imports the seven columns positionally, derives an age group from the age code, deletes records missing selected fields, runs a small quality-check query, and sums the retained counts across authorities.

Its age mapping is:

| Derived group | Source codes | Source ages covered |
|---|---|---|
| 0–4 | 1–2 | 2 and under; 3–4 |
| 5–15 | 3–6 | 5–7; 8–9; 10–14; 15 |
| 16–24 | 7–9 | 16–17; 18–19; 20–24 |
| 25–64 | 10–17 | Eight five-year categories, 25–29 through 60–64 |
| 65+ | 18–23 | 65; 66–69; 70–74; 75–79; 80–84; 85+ |

This mapping is **correct for the supplied code–label pairs** and requires no splitting or estimation.

The aggregation creates ten sex–age-group totals. Each percentage uses the total population of the same sex as its denominator—not the population of the age group or the combined population.

The three created datasets, `ons_population`, `population_by_age_sex` and `population_results`, use one-level names and therefore normally reside in the temporary WORK library. The printed table and chart go to the session’s configured output destination; the script does not explicitly export them.

## 2 What works well

The explicit import definition is a reasonable choice. It avoids guessed types, preserves geographic codes as character identifiers, and uses appropriate numeric reading for the supplied integer counts.

The CSV contains **46 quoted records**, covering the authority name “Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole”. The combination of `DSD` and comma delimiting is appropriate for that embedded comma. `TRUNCOVER` also prevents a short record from consuming values from the following line, while the record-length allowance comfortably exceeds this file’s longest line.

All supplied character values fit their declared input lengths: authority codes are nine characters, the longest authority name is 35, sex labels reach six, and age labels reach 22. All observations are nonmissing, positive integer strings. There are no blank required fields, unexpected field counts or duplicate keys in this file.

The age bands preserve the source categories cleanly. The summary and within-sex percentage calculation are also mathematically appropriate for the stated purpose. Independently calculated results are:

| Age group | Female population | Female % | Male population | Male % |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0–4 | 1,577,358 | 5.2 | 1,654,696 | 5.7 |
| 5–15 | 3,803,829 | 12.5 | 3,995,312 | 13.7 |
| 16–24 | 3,116,309 | 10.2 | 3,202,014 | 11.0 |
| 25–64 | 15,926,041 | 52.4 | 15,258,709 | 52.3 |
| 65+ | 5,996,744 | 19.7 | 5,066,594 | 17.4 |

The combined count is **59,597,606**: 30,420,281 female and 29,177,325 male. These are verified sums of the supplied file, not independently authenticated official national totals.

## 3 Issues and risks

### Confirmed defects and operational limitations

| Issue | Severity | Why it matters | Improved approach |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Configured path does not identify the supplied input folder** ([line 13](Inputs/ons_population_processing.sas:13)) | Medium | The script points to a different directory. As supplied, it will either fail to find the CSV or read a different copy if one exists there. | Configure the input location externally or relative to a defined project root. Check file existence and record the resolved path and checksum. |
| **Unexpected age groups cannot be detected by the current check** ([lines 33–54](Inputs/ons_population_processing.sas:33)) | Medium | Unrecognised or missing age codes are assigned a nonmissing fallback. Checking `missing(age_group)` therefore does not detect them. In addition, `age_group $6` truncates `Unknown` to `Unknow`. No supplied record triggers this defect. | Validate the allowed age codes directly, count unmapped records, and stop or quarantine them. Give any diagnostic label sufficient storage. |
| **Missing records are deleted before being assessed** ([line 44](Inputs/ons_population_processing.sas:44)) | High | The quality check cannot reveal missing counts or identifiers that have already caused deletion. A damaged input could produce understated totals and still appear acceptable. The supplied file has no such records. | Audit the raw import first. Retain rejected records with reasons and reconcile imported, accepted and rejected counts. Fail when required fields are missing unless an explicit policy permits otherwise. |
| **Age groups are ordered alphabetically rather than chronologically** ([line 76](Inputs/ons_population_processing.sas:76)) | Medium | The table explicitly orders character labels as `0-4`, `16-24`, `25-64`, `5-15`, `65+`. The chart also lacks an explicit chronological category order. | Add a numeric age-group order and apply it consistently to both table and chart. Verify the rendered chart. |
| **No explicit persistent deliverables are created** | Medium | Intermediate and final datasets normally disappear with the session. Table and chart destinations depend on session settings, making a completed run difficult to identify and audit. | Define output locations and formats; save the final data, validation results, report, chart and run log together. |

### Missing safeguards and interpretive risks

These are not evidence that the supplied totals are wrong. They are weaknesses that could allow future errors or misleading interpretation.

| Issue | Severity | Why it matters | Improved approach |
|---|---|---|---|
| **No header or structural validation** | Medium | `FIRSTOBS=2` skips the header without checking it, and fields are read by position. Reordered columns or a changed delimiter could corrupt the import. `TRUNCOVER` prevents spillover but does not certify record completeness. | Validate the expected seven headers, their order or explicit mapping, field counts and parsing diagnostics before transformation. |
| **Numeric conversion is not an enforced validation step** | Medium | The numeric informat works for the supplied counts, but invalid text can generate missing numeric values and log diagnostics without stopping the workflow. The resulting population record is then deleted. Negative counts are counted but not blocked; fractional counts are not checked. | Preserve original field text, validate numeric conversion and require finite, nonnegative integers. Make failures stop publication. Document handling of blanks and special missing or suppression markers if future extracts contain them. |
| **No checks for duplicate keys, complete coverage or code–label agreement** | High | Duplicate rows inflate totals; missing authorities or categories reduce them. An altered age codebook could silently change age-group meaning. Aggregation does not expose these problems. | Enforce unique authority–sex–age keys, expected category coverage and one-to-one code–label mappings. Validate geography against a versioned authority list, not only an expected row count. |
| **No reconciliation or authoritative benchmark** | High | An internally consistent national total can still describe the wrong extract, geography or population universe. The “England and Wales” title assumes complete, mutually exclusive coverage. | Reconcile source and grouped totals, compare nation and sex totals with documented benchmarks for the same release, and investigate differences rather than silently adjusting them. |
| **Source provenance is incomplete** | Medium | The comment identifies RM121 and Census 2021, but gives no source URL, download date, release version, geography vintage, extraction filters or population-definition notes. The CSV alone cannot establish these. | Retain the source metadata and original download, with a checksum and extraction details. Document any disclosure-control or rounding guidance applicable to the release. |
| **Chart comparisons need qualification** | Medium | A grouped count chart is valid, but the age bands have very different widths and 65+ is open-ended. A large 25–64 bar partly reflects its much wider age span. Counts also do not show the same comparison as within-sex percentages. | State that bars represent totals over unequal age intervals. Choose counts or percentages to match the analytical question and label the denominator explicitly. |
| **Character encoding is unspecified** | Low | No visible corruption was found, but portability depends on compatible file and session encodings. Character storage limits can also be byte-based. | Document or configure the file encoding and validate decoded labels and byte lengths when moving between environments. |

### Presentation and style—not calculation defects

**Low severity:** the printed table labels the age group and percentage but leaves other headings technical. The chart title omits geography and census year, and the raw sex labels are used without explaining the source definition. More complete labels, a source note and a self-contained title would improve reuse.

The percentage label “Percent within sex” is correct. Displaying one decimal place is reasonable, although the male percentages sum to 100.1% after rounding. That is a presentation effect, not an aggregation error.

An explicit table of age mappings would be easier to review and maintain than an embedded selection block, but the present block is short and readable. This is a maintainability preference, not a reason to reject the current mapping.

## 4 Recommended improvements

The first priority is to make the workflow **fail visibly rather than produce a plausible partial result**. Validate the file identity, header, field structure, numeric conversion, required values, category domains and unique keys before deleting or aggregating anything. Keep an auditable record of every rejection.

The second priority is to formalise the transformation contract. Store the age mapping with its labels and chronological order, validate it against all 23 source categories, and require every input row to map exactly once. Confirm that grouped counts equal accepted source counts, that exactly ten final groups are produced, and that unrounded percentages sum to 100 within each sex.

Automated tests should cover both the supplied data and deliberately damaged examples: a quoted comma, blank observation, invalid number, negative or fractional count, duplicate key, unknown age code, missing category, changed code–label pair and reordered header. These exercise the actual failure paths rather than merely confirming the happy path.

Finally, make each run traceable. Record the input checksum, source metadata, software version, configuration, validation outcomes and output locations. Save durable results and inspect the final table and chart for age ordering, complete titles, readable labels and denominator clarity.

**The supplied totals are useful regression-test expectations**, but they are not a substitute for an independently sourced benchmark.

## 5 Open-source implementation principles

An open-source implementation could improve portability, reviewability and automation, but changing technology would not itself fix the weaknesses identified above.

A robust design would separate ingestion, validation, transformation, aggregation and presentation. Ingestion should use a standards-aware reader with explicit handling of quoted delimiters, missing-value conventions, encoding and conversion failures. Schema validation should enforce required columns, types, category domains, identifiers and key uniqueness before analytical processing begins.

Reusable transformations should accept validated data and a versioned age-mapping specification rather than depend on session state or hard-coded locations. Automated tests should check both expected results and intentional failures. Paths, reporting options and output destinations should be configurable without editing core processing logic.

Data provenance should travel with the outputs: source location, release details, extraction settings, checksum and run timestamp. A reproducible environment should record the required software versions so the same inputs and configuration can be rerun consistently.

Transparent deliverables would include machine-readable results, a validation summary, a human-readable report and accessible visualisation. Charts should preserve chronological age order, explain unequal age-band widths, use readable labels and adequate contrast, and remain understandable without colour alone. An accompanying table or text description should communicate the same information.

The current SAS approach still has reasonable foundations: explicit field definitions, staged processing, a short deterministic age mapping, a standard grouped summary and a correctly defined percentage denominator. **Most recommended safeguards can also be added within SAS.** The case for an open-source alternative is principally about the surrounding engineering, access and deployment needs—not a mathematical deficiency in these summary procedures.

## 6 Overall assessment

**This is a sound small-example transformation, but not yet a dependable production workflow.** For the supplied CSV, the input lengths are adequate, quoted commas are appropriately handled, the age mapping is correct, and the aggregation and percentage formula are appropriate.

The most important weaknesses are ineffective validation, deletion before audit, absent coverage and reconciliation checks, nonchronological age ordering, and limited provenance and output persistence. None demonstrates that the supplied population sums are wrong; together, however, they mean that a changed or damaged input could generate convincing but incorrect output.

The practical next step is to retain the simple analytical core while adding explicit validation gates, chronological ordering, benchmark reconciliation and durable, traceable deliverables.

# Prioritised validation and acceptance checklist

Use **P0 as correctness gates**, **P1 as operational-release requirements**, and **P2 as presentation and maintenance improvements**. A failed gate should prevent publication—not merely produce a warning in a log.

The reference values below come from the earlier inspection of the supplied CSV. They are regression-test expectations, **not independently authenticated official benchmarks**.

## P0 — Block publication if any check fails

| Done | Validation | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **Input identity** | The configured path resolves to the intended CSV. Record its resolved location and checksum; fail if the file is absent. |
| ☐ | **Schema and headers** | Exactly the seven expected columns are present. Either enforce their order or map them explicitly by validated names. |
| ☐ | **CSV parsing** | Every record has seven fields, with no unresolved parsing errors. The quoted name “Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole” remains one field. |
| ☐ | **Required values** | No missing or blank authority code, authority name, sex code or label, age code or label, or observation. Inspect these **before deleting any records**. |
| ☐ | **Numeric validity** | Every observation converts successfully to a finite, nonnegative integer. Missing or invalid numeric text cannot silently become an excluded record. Zero is permitted unless the source specification says otherwise. |
| ☐ | **Category validity** | Sex codes and labels match the supplied codebook. Age codes are exactly the permitted 1–23 values, with matching source labels. No unmapped category is accepted. |
| ☐ | **Unique keys** | There are zero duplicate authority–sex–age keys. Duplicates cause investigation, not automatic deduplication. |
| ☐ | **Coverage** | Authorities match a documented geography list for the intended release. Every authority has both sexes and all 23 age categories, with no unexpected total or overlapping geography rows. |
| ☐ | **Age mapping** | Every permitted source category maps exactly once to the intended broad age group. Boundary cases—including ages 15, 16, 24, 25, 64 and 65—map correctly. Unknown codes fail validation rather than becoming a report category. |
| ☐ | **Record accountability** | Imported records equal accepted plus rejected records. Rejections retain their original values and reasons. For this supplied file, expect zero rejections. |
| ☐ | **Aggregation reconciliation** | Grand totals and totals within sex are unchanged by age grouping. The final result contains exactly two sexes × five age groups, with unique output keys. |
| ☐ | **Percentage calculation** | Each percentage uses its own sex’s total as denominator; denominators are positive. Unrounded percentages sum to 100 within each sex, within a documented numerical tolerance. |
| ☐ | **Source reconciliation** | Totals are compared with an authoritative benchmark for the same release, geography and population definition. Every discrepancy has a documented explanation and approved tolerance. |
| ☐ | **Chronological order** | Both the table and rendered chart show `0–4`, `5–15`, `16–24`, `25–64`, `65+`, in that order. |

### Regression expectations for this supplied extract

Apply these exact expectations only to the same input version. A new release requires review and approval of new expectations.

| Check | Expected result |
|---|---:|
| Data records | 15,226 |
| Authorities | 331 |
| English / Welsh authorities, by code prefix | 309 / 22 |
| Records per authority | 46 |
| Duplicate authority–sex–age keys | 0 |
| Missing required values | 0 |
| Invalid, negative or fractional observations | 0 |
| Female population | 30,420,281 |
| Male population | 29,177,325 |
| Combined population | **59,597,606** |

The ten age-group counts should also match the independently calculated results in the review. Rounded percentages need not sum to exactly 100: the supplied male percentages sum to 100.1% at one decimal place.

## P1 — Required before routine or shared use

| Done | Validation | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **Effective failure handling** | A failed P0 check stops report generation and returns an identifiable failed-run status. Old outputs cannot be mistaken for new successful results. |
| ☐ | **Adverse-input tests** | Automated tests deliberately introduce a quoted comma, short record, reordered header, missing value, invalid number, negative or fractional count, duplicate key, unknown age code and missing category. Each is handled according to its specified policy. |
| ☐ | **Import capacity and encoding** | Encoding is documented; labels decode correctly. Character storage and record lengths accommodate the validated input without truncation. Any fallback diagnostic label also fits its field. |
| ☐ | **Source provenance** | Retain the original input, source location, download date, release/version, extraction filters, geography vintage and population-definition notes. Record applicable disclosure-control guidance. |
| ☐ | **Configurable paths** | Input and output locations are configuration values, not personal absolute paths embedded in processing logic. |
| ☐ | **Persistent deliverables** | Save final data, validation results, report, chart and run log to explicit locations. Clearly distinguish successful, failed and superseded runs. |
| ☐ | **Reproducible execution** | Record software versions and configuration. A fresh session can reproduce the same numerical results without relying on existing session objects or manual steps. |
| ☐ | **Output semantics** | Tables and charts identify geography, census year, source, population measure and percentage denominator. Sex categories retain their source meaning. |
| ☐ | **Visual accessibility and interpretation** | Inspect the rendered chart for readable labels, chronological order, sufficient contrast and interpretation without colour alone. Explain that age groups have unequal widths and that 65+ is open-ended. Provide an accompanying data table. |
| ☐ | **Independent sign-off** | A reviewer confirms the mapping, benchmark reconciliation, percentage denominator and rendered outputs. Record approval against the run or version. |

## P2 — Improve maintainability and clarity

| Done | Improvement | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **Centralise the age mapping** | One reviewable specification contains source codes, source labels, reporting groups and sort order; processing and presentation use the same specification. |
| ☐ | **Separate processing stages** | Ingestion, validation, transformation, aggregation and presentation can be tested independently. |
| ☐ | **Use reader-friendly headings** | Replace technical output headings with clear labels and include a rounding note where appropriate. |
| ☐ | **Document operation and ownership** | A short run guide explains configuration, expected outputs, failure investigation and who approves source or mapping changes. |

## Acceptance decision

| Decision | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Reject / investigate** | Any P0 gate fails or remains unresolved. |
| **Accept for a controlled exercise** | All P0 gates pass; any incomplete P1 requirements are explicitly documented, with use restricted accordingly. |
| **Accept for routine use** | All P0 and P1 requirements pass, with retained evidence and reviewer approval. |
| **Maintenance backlog** | Remaining P2 items have owners and do not conceal unresolved correctness risks. |

**On the earlier review evidence, the workflow is not yet ready for routine acceptance.** The CSV passed several structural checks, but the script does not enforce them; benchmark reconciliation remains unverified, and the ordering, audit and operational requirements still need attention.

# Population-processing workflow: test specification

**Scope:** ingestion, validation, age grouping, aggregation and reporting for [ons_population_processing.sas](Inputs/ons_population_processing.sas) and [ons_rm121_sex_by_age_2021.csv](Inputs/ons_rm121_sex_by_age_2021.csv).

**Execution status:** This is a specification, not a test-execution report. All tests begin as **Not run**. Reference values come from the earlier file inspection; they have not been independently reconciled to an official benchmark.

## 1. Test execution and evidence records

Maintain one execution record per test per run.

| Field | Required content |
|---|---|
| Run ID | Unique identifier linking all tests and outputs from one execution |
| Test ID | Identifier from the tables below |
| Execution date and tester | Timestamp and responsible person or automated process |
| Code version | Version identifier or checksum of the processing script |
| Input identity | Resolved file path, checksum and source-release identifier |
| Environment and configuration | Software versions, encoding, configured paths and relevant options |
| Actual outcome | Observed values, diagnostic messages or behaviour |
| Status | Not run, Pass, Fail, Blocked or Not applicable |
| Evidence reference | Durable path to logs, validation tables, comparisons or rendered output |
| Defect / disposition | Issue reference, investigation outcome and any approved exception |
| Reviewer | Reviewer identity and approval date, where required |

A **Pass requires retained evidence**. “Blocked” and “Not run” do not count as passes. “Not applicable” requires a documented rationale and reviewer approval.

For every deliberately invalid input, retain the fixture, its checksum and the exact mutation from the baseline. An expected validation failure counts as a test pass only if the workflow detects the intended problem and prevents publication.

## 2. P0 — Correctness and publication gates

### Input and schema

| Test ID | Test / procedure | Expected outcome | Required evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| P0-01 | Resolve the configured input; repeat with a nonexistent path. | Baseline resolves to the intended file. Missing-file run stops before processing and identifies the unresolved path. | Resolved path, checksum and both run logs. |
| P0-02 | Validate all seven headers. Test a renamed, missing and additional column separately. | Baseline passes. Each incompatible schema is rejected before transformation. | Expected-versus-observed schema and failure diagnostics. |
| P0-03 | Reorder input columns. | Either values are mapped correctly by validated headers, or the changed order is explicitly rejected. Positional misinterpretation is never accepted. | Fixture, import comparison or rejection log. |
| P0-04 | Parse the supplied quoted authority name; separately introduce a malformed quoted field and a short record. | “Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole” remains one field. Malformed or incomplete records are rejected without absorbing values from another record. | Parsed-field extract, record-level diagnostics and run status. |
| P0-05 | Introduce a blank into each required field in separate fixtures. | Each missing value is detected before deletion or aggregation. The affected record and reason are retained; publication is blocked. | Validation counts, rejected-record extracts and failure status. |
| P0-06 | Test valid zero, invalid numeric text, a negative value, a fraction and a missing observation separately. | Zero is accepted unless the documented source contract prohibits it. Other cases fail the count-validity rule; no failed conversion silently disappears. | Original text, conversion result and validation diagnostics. |
| P0-07 | Introduce an unknown sex code, mismatched sex label, unknown age code and mismatched age label separately. | Each invalid code or code–label pair is rejected. No fallback age group reaches published results. | Domain-check results and offending records. |

### Coverage and transformation

| Test ID | Test / procedure | Expected outcome | Required evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| P0-08 | Check key uniqueness; add one duplicate authority–sex–age record. | Baseline has zero duplicates. Duplicate fixture fails before aggregation; records are not silently deduplicated. | Duplicate-key report and failure log. |
| P0-09 | Compare authorities with the approved geography list. Remove one expected authority and add an unexpected authority in separate fixtures. | Baseline matches the approved list. Missing, unexpected or overlapping geographies are detected. | Versioned reference list and set-difference report. |
| P0-10 | Check the complete sex–age grid within each authority; remove one combination. | Every authority has exactly both sexes × 23 ages. The missing combination is identified and blocks publication. | Completeness matrix and missing-key report. |
| P0-11 | Evaluate all 23 age-code mappings against an independently reviewed mapping specification. | Every valid source code maps exactly once to the correct group, with no gaps or overlaps. | Expected-versus-actual mapping for all codes. |
| P0-12 | Reconcile imported, accepted and rejected records, including an invalid-record fixture. | Imported = accepted + rejected, with no double counting or unexplained loss. Baseline has 15,226 accepted and zero rejected records. | Row-accounting table and rejection register. |
| P0-13 | Compare counts before and after grouping, overall and within sex. | Totals are unchanged. Final keys are unique and there are exactly ten sex–age-group rows. | Reconciliation table with zero differences. |
| P0-14 | Independently recompute each percentage. Test a fixture with a zero sex-total denominator. | Percentages equal count ÷ same-sex total × 100. Unrounded sums differ from 100 by no more than a specified tolerance, such as 0.00000001 percentage points. A zero denominator blocks publication. | Independent calculations, tolerance checks and failure log. |
| P0-15 | Compare the unchanged baseline with the regression values below. | All population counts and structural counts match exactly. Display percentages match the documented rounding rule. | Machine-readable expected-versus-actual comparison. |
| P0-16 | Reconcile with an authoritative benchmark for the same release and population definition. | Totals match the benchmark or every difference is explained against an approved source-specific tolerance. Unexplained differences block publication. | Benchmark source, metadata, comparison and approval. |
| P0-17 | Inspect table row order and rendered chart order. | Both show 0–4, 5–15, 16–24, 25–64, 65+. | Ordered output extract and rendered chart. |

### Age-mapping oracle for P0-11

| Source codes | Expected group | Boundary coverage |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | 0–4 | Includes ages 0 through 4 |
| 3–6 | 5–15 | Includes age 15 |
| 7–9 | 16–24 | Begins at 16; ends at 24 |
| 10–17 | 25–64 | Begins at 25; ends at 64 |
| 18–23 | 65+ | Includes age 65 and the open-ended oldest category |

The input contains age categories, not individual ages. Boundary tests must therefore validate the corresponding source codes **and labels**, rather than invent single-year observations.

### Baseline oracle for P0-15

| Measure | Expected value |
|---|---:|
| Input records | 15,226 |
| Authorities | 331 |
| English / Welsh authorities by code prefix | 309 / 22 |
| Records per authority | 46 |
| Duplicate keys / rejected records | 0 / 0 |
| Female total | 30,420,281 |
| Male total | 29,177,325 |
| Combined total | 59,597,606 |

| Age group | Female count | Female displayed % | Male count | Male displayed % |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0–4 | 1,577,358 | 5.2 | 1,654,696 | 5.7 |
| 5–15 | 3,803,829 | 12.5 | 3,995,312 | 13.7 |
| 16–24 | 3,116,309 | 10.2 | 3,202,014 | 11.0 |

The displayed male percentages total 100.1% because of rounding; this must not cause failure of an otherwise correct result. Baseline expectations must not be updated merely to make a failing test pass.

## 3. P1 — Operational-release requirements

| Test ID | Test / procedure | Expected outcome | Required evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1-01 | Trigger a P0 failure after an earlier successful run. | Run is clearly marked failed. No new successful report is published, and earlier outputs cannot be mistaken for the failed run’s results. | Run statuses, output inventory and publication log. |
| P1-02 | Execute the full adverse-input suite automatically. | Every fixture triggers its specified result; the suite reports failures reliably and checks diagnostic reasons, not only generic failure status. | Test-suite report and fixture manifest. |
| P1-03 | Test declared encoding, accented text and field-length limits. | Valid text is preserved. Unsupported encoding or excessive length is reported; no silent truncation occurs, including for diagnostic labels. | Before-and-after values, byte lengths and logs. |
| P1-04 | Review provenance completeness. | Source location, download date, release, filters, geography vintage, population definition and applicable disclosure-control notes are recorded. | Provenance manifest and retained source metadata. |
| P1-05 | Run from two configured locations, including a path containing spaces. | The same input produces the same numerical results without editing processing logic. | Configurations, logs and output comparison. |
| P1-06 | End the processing session and retrieve deliverables. | Final data, validation report, chart, report and log remain accessible at documented locations. | Output manifest, checksums and retrieval check. |
| P1-07 | Repeat in a clean session using the recorded environment. | No dependence on pre-existing objects or manual steps. Numerical outputs match; variable timestamps or document metadata are excluded from comparison. | Environment record and reproducibility comparison. |
| P1-08 | Review titles, headings and notes. | Outputs identify geography, census year, source, count measure, within-sex denominator and rounding policy; category wording preserves source meaning. | Completed presentation review and rendered outputs. |
| P1-09 | Review chart accessibility and interpretation. | Labels are readable, groups are distinguishable without colour alone, unequal age widths are explained, and an equivalent table or text description is available. | Accessibility review and final artefacts. |
| P1-10 | Conduct independent acceptance review. | Reviewer approves the mapping, benchmark reconciliation, denominator and final outputs; unresolved failures remain visible. | Signed acceptance record tied to the run and code version. |

## 4. P2 — Maintainability and documentation

| Test ID | Test / procedure | Expected outcome | Required evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| P2-01 | Trace mapping and ordering definitions. | A single reviewable specification governs source categories, reporting groups and chronological order. | Mapping specification and implementation references. |
| P2-02 | Test processing stages independently. | Ingestion, validation, transformation, aggregation and presentation have defined inputs and outputs and can be tested separately. | Stage-level test results. |
| P2-03 | Ask another operator to follow the run guide. | They can configure and run the workflow, locate outputs and investigate a deliberately failed run without undocumented assistance. | Operator walkthrough record and documentation issues. |
| P2-04 | Review ownership and change control. | Owners and approval requirements exist for source changes, mapping changes and baseline updates. | Ownership record and change-control procedure. |

## 5. Acceptance rules

| Decision | Required result |
|---|---|
| **Reject / investigate** | Any P0 test is failed, blocked or not run. |
| **Controlled-exercise acceptance** | All P0 tests pass. Incomplete P1 requirements have documented restrictions, owners and approval. |
| **Routine-use acceptance** | All applicable P0 and P1 tests pass, supporting evidence is retained, and independent approval is recorded. |
| **Maintenance backlog** | Outstanding P2 items have owners and target dates and do not conceal a correctness or operational-release failure. |

**No acceptance decision is established by this specification alone.** Execution records, an approved geography reference and authoritative benchmark reconciliation are still required.

1-93]\n1\t/*\n2\t  ONS Census 2021: population processin...[truncated, total 3447 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 3.1KB, 93 lines, showing lines 1-93]\n/*\n  ONS Census 2021: population processing example\n  Source data: RM121, Sex by age, England and Wales (ONS).\n\n  This program imports the accompanying CSV, assigns broad age bands,\n  performs simple quality checks, and creates England-and-Wales totals and\n  percentages by sex and age band.\n\n  In SAS Studio: upload both files to the same folder, then replace data_dir\n  below with that folder's path.\n*/\n\n%let data_dir=/Users/alex/Documents/Codex/2026-11-19/ca/outputs;\n\nfilename onsin \"&data_dir./ons_rm121_sex_by_age_2021.csv\";\n\n/* Import explicitly so the program does not depend on PROC IMPORT guessing\n   column types or variable names from the CSV headers. */\ndata ons_population;\n    infile onsin dsd dlm=',' firstobs=2 lrecl=1048576 truncover;\n    length la_code $9 la_name $80 sex $6 age_band $30 age_group $6;\n    informat sex_code age_code population best32.;\n    format population comma15.;\n\n    input la_code :$9.\n          la_name :$80.\n          sex_code :best32.\n          sex :$6.\n          age_code :best32.\n          age_band :$30.\n          population :best32.;\n\n    /* Convert the ONS 23 age categories into common reporting bands. */\n    select (age_code);\n        when (1, 2)                     age_group = '0-4';\n        when (3, 4, 5, 6)               age_group = '5-15';\n        when (7, 8, 9)                  age_group = '16-24';\n        when (10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15,\n              16, 17)                   age_group = '25-64';\n        when (18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23)   age_group = '65+';\n        otherwise                       age_group = 'Unknown';\n    end;\n\n    if missing(la_code) or missing(sex) or missing(population) then delete;\nrun;\n\n/* Quality check: there should be no missing or negative counts. */\nproc sql;\n    title 'Data-quality check';\n    select count(*) as records format=comma12.,\n           sum(missing(age_group)) as missing_age_groups,\n           sum(population \u003c 0) as negative_counts\n    from ons_population;\nquit;\n\n/* Aggregate the local-authority records to England-and-Wales totals. */\nproc summary data=ons_population nway;\n    class sex age_group;\n    var population;\n    output out=population_by_age_sex(drop=_type_ _freq_) sum=population;\nrun;\n\nproc sql;\n    create table population_results as\n    select a.sex,\n           a.age_group,\n           a.population format=comma15. as population,\n           100 * a.population / b.total_population\n               as percent_of_sex format=5.1\n    from population_by_age_sex as a\n    inner join\n      (select sex, sum(population) as total_population\n       from population_by_age_sex\n       group by sex) as b\n    on a.sex = b.sex\n    order by sex, a.age_group;\nquit;\n\ntitle 'England and Wales population by sex and broad age group, Census 2021';\nproc print data=population_results noobs label;\n    label age_group='Age group'\n          percent_of_sex='Percent within sex';\nrun;\n\nproc sgplot data=population_by_age_sex;\n    vbar age_group / response=population group=sex groupdisplay=cluster;\n    yaxis grid label='Population';\n    xaxis label='Age group';\n    title 'Population totals by sex and broad age group';\nrun;\n\ntitle;\n"},"elapsedMs":12}</script></tool-result></div>

## Discovery

Root: `/Users/alex/Documents/Code/AI-PoC`

- `Inputs/ons_population_processing.sas` — complete 93-line SAS workflow.
- `Inputs/ons_rm121_sex_by_age_2021.csv` — seven-column ONS input; headers and example age categories are at lines 1–24.
- `README.md:1` contains only the project title; `.gitignore:1–4` ignores standard R session files.
- No existing review, report, test-specification documents, R scripts, R project file, dependency lockfile, or R workflow infrastructure were found. The unrelated prompt collection was not read.

## SAS workflow

The script reads the CSV positionally with explicit types and fixed character widths (`Inputs/ons_population_processing.sas:13–31`). It maps age codes 1–23 into five broad bands, deletes rows missing authority code, sex, or population, and reports missing age groups and negative counts (`:33–54`). It then sums population by sex and age group, calculates percentages **within sex**, prints a table, and draws a clustered bar chart (`:56–90`). It does not write output files.

## Planning implications

**Required corrections**
- Replace the hard-coded, obsolete input directory (`:13–15`) with a portable, configurable path.
- Validate input types and required fields before discarding records; report or fail on invalid data rather than silently deleting it (`:44`).
- Detect unexpected age codes explicitly: `Unknown` is assigned to a six-character variable and is therefore truncated; the subsequent missing-age check does not detect it (`:21, 33–41, 47–53`).
- Treat negative counts as actionable validation failures, not merely a printed count (`:47–54`). Preserve the within-sex denominator and verify it is nonzero (`:63–76`).
- Define chronological age-band ordering rather than relying on the SAS character sort (`:76`).

**Optional enhancements**
- Structure a tidyverse-first replacement as separate import, validation, transformation, aggregation, and presentation functions; add focused tests for mapping boundaries, invalid records, totals, and percentage denominators.
- Add reproducible dependency management and optional saved tables or plots; no existing project convention requires a particular choice.

# Implementation plan: reusable R population-processing workflow

## 1. Recommended approach and scope

Retain the current workflow’s analytical purpose: combine local-authority population counts into the five agreed age groups and calculate percentages **within each sex**. Replace its weak validation and session-dependent operation with a modular, Tidyverse-first R workflow.

The main benefit should be **more reliable evidence and clearer processing contracts**, not a more complicated calculation.

This plan is grounded in the earlier code-and-data review and test specification. The SAS source was inspected, but SAS was not executed. The previously calculated totals are regression references for the supplied CSV, not independently authenticated official benchmarks.

| Delivery class | Scope |
|---|---|
| **Required corrections** | Eliminate silent record loss; validate schema, conversions, categories, keys and coverage; enforce correct age ordering; reconcile aggregation and denominators. |
| **Required for routine use** | Configurable paths, persistent outputs, automated tests, provenance, reproducible dependencies, operating instructions and review evidence. |
| **Optional enhancements** | Interactive outputs, richer reporting, automated scheduling, continuous integration, packaged distribution and additional real datasets. |

Use **readr** for ingestion, **dplyr** and **tidyr** for validation and transformation, and **ggplot2** for visualisation. Use **testthat** for automated tests and **renv** for dependency recording. Additional tools should be introduced only where they solve an agreed need.

An ordinary R project with small functions is sufficient initially; an R package or elaborate orchestration framework is not yet justified.

## 2. Proposed components

### A. Configuration and file paths

**Purpose and interface.** Accept an analysis configuration and explicit project root. Return validated settings for source files, schema, reference tables, geography, classification, aggregation, percentage denominators and output locations.

**Findings addressed.** The SAS script contains a personal absolute path and leaves important assumptions embedded in processing and presentation.

**Design responsibility.** Use a reusable configuration reader and validator, with analysis-specific settings stored separately. A human-readable configuration file is appropriate; YAML is a reasonable proposed format. Keep mappings and reference data in versioned tables rather than embedding long lists in configuration.

**Safeguards.** Check required settings, input existence and resolved paths before processing. Prevent output locations from overwriting source data. Reject contradictory grouping or denominator settings. Resolve paths against the declared project root rather than relying on the current IDE directory.

**Explicit assumptions.** Initially, one run processes one selected release. Scheduling, shared-server execution and credentials are not established requirements. Exact baseline totals belong in regression tests, not universal configuration rules.

### B. Data ingestion and schema checks

**Purpose and interface.** Accept the configured CSV and schema. Return preserved source values, a canonical tibble, source-record identifiers and parsing diagnostics.

**Findings addressed.** The current import reads columns positionally, skips rather than validates the header, and does not turn conversion problems into publication-blocking failures.

**Design responsibility.** Build reusable ingestion and schema-validation functions, with a source-specific adapter mapping original headers to canonical names. Initially read fields as character, preserving their original contents, then explicitly parse observations. This separates malformed file structure from invalid analytical values.

**Safeguards.** Validate required, duplicate and unexpected headers. Map columns by validated names so harmless column reordering does not corrupt values. Set delimiter, quote handling, encoding and missing-value conventions explicitly. Inspect parser diagnostics and reject malformed or incomplete records. Preserve codes as character identifiers, including leading zeros.

Test the supplied quoted authority name containing a comma. Do not assume that “successfully read” means “valid dataset”.

**Explicit assumptions.** The initial input is a seven-column CSV. Its encoding and any permitted suppression or missing-value markers need confirmation. Numeric counts should use a representation that avoids ordinary integer overflow while remaining exact within the agreed range; never silently round fractional values into counts.

### C. Cleaning and raw-data validation

**Purpose and interface.** Accept parsed observations and approved reference tables. Return validated data and a structured validation report, retaining invalid records with reasons.

**Findings addressed.** The SAS program deletes incomplete records before auditing them, checks too few fields and does not validate duplicates, complete category coverage or code–label consistency.

**Design responsibility.** Provide reusable validators for required values, numeric domains, category domains, code–label relationships, unique keys and expected combinations. Dataset-specific contracts determine which categories and combinations are required.

**Safeguards.** For this extract, missing required values, failed conversions, nonfinite values, negative or fractional counts, unknown categories, duplicate keys and incomplete coverage should block publication. Zero counts should remain valid unless the source contract says otherwise.

Do not silently deduplicate, impute, discard records or treat missing counts as zero. Reconcile imported records to accepted and rejected records. Preserve original labels; permit only documented normalisations.

**Explicit assumptions.** A complete two-sex × 23-age grid is appropriate for the supplied extract, not necessarily every future official dataset. Sparse tables, suppression and “not applicable” observations require explicit source-specific policies.

### D. Reusable category derivation

**Purpose and interface.** Accept validated source categories and a versioned mapping table. Return reporting-category identifiers, labels and ordering, while retaining source categories for traceability.

**Findings addressed.** The current mapping depends on numeric codes without validating their labels, its fallback is truncated, and the missing-age-group check cannot detect unmapped categories.

**Design responsibility.** Use a reusable many-to-one category-mapping function. The present age mapping is analysis-specific reference data:

| Source age codes | Reporting group |
|---|---|
| 1–2 | 0–4 |
| 3–6 | 5–15 |
| 7–9 | 16–24 |
| 10–17 | 25–64 |
| 18–23 | 65+ |

Each mapping should identify its applicable source classification and version and include an explicit numeric reporting order.

**Safeguards.** Require unique mapping keys and complete coverage. Check that the join neither duplicates nor loses records and preserves population totals. Unmatched categories should fail validation, not become an accepted “Unknown” group.

Test all 23 code–label mappings, especially the source categories containing ages 15, 16, 24, 25, 64 and 65.

**Explicit assumptions.** The current source categories fit the target bands exactly. Future source categories crossing a reporting boundary cannot be split accurately without finer data or additional assumptions. Such redistribution is outside the proposed initial scope.

### E. Aggregation and percentages

**Purpose and interface.** Accept validated, mapped counts and an analysis specification. Return tidy population totals, denominator values and full-precision percentages.

**Findings addressed.** The existing calculation is reasonable, but total preservation, geography compatibility and denominator validity are not enforced.

**Design responsibility.** Use reusable aggregation and percentage functions with explicit grouping and denominator dimensions. The current analysis-specific step selects the England-and-Wales scope and aggregates mutually exclusive authorities by sex and reporting age group.

Keep release, observation period, geography version, measure and classification context attached to results.

**Safeguards.** Reconcile counts before and after mapping and aggregation, overall and within sex. Require unique final keys and the expected ten result rows for this extract. Denominators must be positive. Unrounded percentages must sum to 100 within each sex within a documented numerical tolerance.

Do not pool different periods or releases, sum overlapping geography levels, average percentages or hide missing observations during summation.

**Explicit assumptions.** Counts are additive over the selected authorities and categories. Complete, nonoverlapping national coverage requires independent verification. Aggregation to other geography levels needs a compatible authoritative lookup; boundary harmonisation is a separate problem.

### F. Tabular outputs and visualisations

**Purpose and interface.** Accept validated results and presentation metadata. Produce machine-readable data, a readable summary table and an accessible chart.

**Findings addressed.** Current outputs are session-dependent, age ordering is incorrect, headings are partly technical and the chart lacks complete context.

**Design responsibility.** Use reusable formatting and export helpers, with analysis-specific titles, notes and chart choices. Proposed minimum formats are CSV, a simple HTML summary and PNG; confirm these with intended users before fixing the output contract.

**Safeguards.** Apply chronological ordering explicitly in both tables and charts. Include geography, census year, units, source and percentage denominator. Keep exported analytical values numeric and full precision; round only for presentation.

Explain unequal age-band widths and the open-ended 65+ group. The existing clustered count chart remains reasonable, but it should not imply age-specific concentration independent of band width. Provide an equivalent table and readable text description, with adequate contrast and distinctions that do not depend only on colour.

**Explicit assumptions.** A percentage chart could be an optional additional view, not a silent replacement for counts. A dashboard or formal publishing system is not currently required.

### G. Quality assurance and automated checks

**Purpose and interface.** Accept functions, fixtures, expected results and runtime data. Produce automated test results, validation summaries and a clear publication decision.

**Findings addressed.** The current checks report limited problems without stopping processing; there is no adverse-input suite, independent benchmark reconciliation or retained acceptance evidence.

**Design responsibility.** Use testthat for unit, integration and regression tests. Preserve the earlier P0/P1/P2 test IDs in test descriptions or a traceability table. Separate development tests from runtime validation: passing tests does not certify a newly supplied file.

**Safeguards.** Test valid inputs and deliberately damaged fixtures: reordered headers, quoted commas, missing fields, malformed numbers, negative and fractional counts, unknown codes, duplicates, incomplete combinations, failed joins and zero denominators.

Tests should verify the intended diagnostic reason, not merely any error. Expected mappings should be independently reviewed rather than generated using the same transformation under test. Failed runs must not publish new “successful” outputs or make old outputs appear current.

**Explicit assumptions.** Prior independent calculations provide regression expectations, not official certification. A side-by-side SAS run is optional if an environment is available; exact equivalence cannot currently be claimed.

### H. Documentation and reproducibility

**Purpose and interface.** Capture source, configuration, methods, environment and results. Produce operating instructions, a data dictionary, methodology notes, a decision log and a run manifest.

**Findings addressed.** Source provenance is incomplete, outputs are not durable and successful execution depends on undocumented session settings.

**Design responsibility.** Use consistent `snake_case` names. Suggested canonical columns include `geography_code`, `geography_name`, `sex_code`, `sex_label`, `source_age_code`, `source_age_label` and `population`. Preserve the original headers in metadata.

Document each function’s inputs, outputs, constraints, failure conditions and side effects. Inline comments should explain source assumptions and non-obvious decisions—not repeat the code. User instructions should explain setup, configuration, execution, outputs and failure investigation.

**Safeguards.** Record source checksum, resolved paths, configuration, reference-table versions, code version, R and dependency versions, validation outcomes and output checksums. Use unique run directories and retain failed-run diagnostics. Record dependencies with renv and verify a fresh-session run.

**Explicit assumptions.** Unknown source metadata must remain explicitly unknown. Do not infer an exact observation date from the filename. Agree retention and version-control policies rather than automatically committing downloads or generated outputs. No random seed is needed for a deterministic workflow.

## 3. Proposed folder structure

The structure below is proposed, not already created. Preserve the existing source files unchanged in [Inputs/](Inputs/).

```text
AI-PoC/
  README.md
  Inputs/                       # Original CSV and reference SAS
  config/                       # Dataset-specific settings and schema
  reference/
    age_mappings/
    geographies/
    benchmarks/
  R/
    configuration.R
    ingestion.R
    validation.R
    category_mapping.R
    summarisation.R
    presentation.R
    provenance.R
  scripts/
    run_population_analysis.R   # Thin entry point
  tests/
    testthat/
    fixtures/                   # Small valid and invalid examples
    expected/                   # Reviewed regression results
  docs/
    data_dictionary.md
    methodology.md
    source_provenance.md
    test_specification.md
    decisions.md
    developer_guide.md
  outputs/
    <run-id>/
      data/
      tables/
      figures/
      validation/
      logs/
      manifest.json
  renv.lock
```

Keep shared logic in functions and the entry script short. File boundaries may be simplified during design review; an arbitrary number of files is not a goal.

## 4. Supporting future population datasets

Reuse should come from separating **source adapters, contracts and reference data** from common calculations.

| Dataset variation | Configuration or adapter change | Important limit |
|---|---|---|
| Different geography level | Supply geography level/version, approved coverage and compatible parent lookup | Overlapping areas or changing boundaries cannot simply be summed |
| Different age classification | Supply a versioned exact mapping and reporting order | Coarse categories cannot produce finer groups without extra information |
| Different sex categories | Supply the permitted domain, labels, order and classification identifier | Do not equate sex with gender or sum “all persons” alongside component categories |
| Different observation periods | Retain period as an explicit dimension and validate coverage within period | Do not sum population snapshots across time by default |
| Suppressed observations | Define source-specific value-status and publication rules | Never treat suppression as zero or silently calculate incomplete percentages |
| Different measures | Supply units and an approved aggregation contract | Rates and percentages do not share the aggregation rules of counts |

A small alternative fixture can demonstrate that the design is not intrinsically tied to two sexes, 23 source categories or 2021. Delivering another real dataset is an optional extension.

## 5. Questions to resolve before implementation

| Uncertainty | Question and implementation consequence |
|---|---|
| Source provenance | What is the original download location, release, extraction and population definition? Preserve the supplied file, but do not invent missing metadata. |
| Geography | Which official geography vintage and authority list apply? Observing 331 authorities does not independently prove complete coverage. |
| Authoritative benchmark | Which published totals are comparable, and are any discrepancies expected? Agree tolerances only from source evidence. |
| Analytical contract | Are the existing five groups and within-sex percentages the confirmed target? The plan preserves them provisionally. |
| Encoding and missingness | What encoding and missing/suppression markers are permitted? These determine parsing and validation rules. |
| Operation and outputs | Who will run the workflow, on which systems, and which output formats are needed? A static project-based workflow is the proposed minimum. |
| Storage and ownership | Where should evidence be retained, for how long, and who approves source, mapping and baseline changes? |
| SAS comparison | Is reproducing the analytical intent sufficient, or is an executed side-by-side comparison required? SAS availability has not been established. |

Generic implementation can begin after interfaces and validation policies are agreed, even while an external benchmark is being obtained. **Routine acceptance must remain blocked if required reconciliation evidence is unresolved.**

## 6. Phased delivery plan and acceptance criteria

### Delivery phases

| Phase | Deliverables | Review gate |
|---|---|---|
| **0 — Pre-code agreement** | Approve schema, configuration approach, mappings, denominator, output contract and error policy. Assign owners to unresolved evidence questions. | Separate coding blockers from release blockers; do not silently convert assumptions into requirements. |
| **1 — Minimum viable implementation** | Strict ingestion, validation, mapping, aggregation, percentages, ordered table/chart, explicit outputs, basic provenance and essential automated tests. | Supplied input matches reviewed calculations; invalid inputs block publication; no silent exclusions. |
| **2 — Routine-use hardening** | Complete adverse-input tests, authoritative reconciliation, dependency recording, run manifests, fresh-session reproduction, documentation and accessibility review. | All applicable P0 and P1 requirements pass with retained evidence and independent sign-off. |
| **3 — Reuse verification** | Exercise an alternative classification or period using small fixtures. | Compatible changes require configuration/reference updates, not rewrites; incompatible inputs fail clearly. |
| **4 — Optional enhancements** | Consider richer reports, additional datasets, continuous integration, scheduling or packaged distribution. | Approve separately against demonstrated user needs. |

### Suggested finished-workflow acceptance criteria

| Area | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|
| Source integrity | Intended input is identified by path and checksum; original data remain unchanged. |
| Raw-data validity | Schema, parsing, required values, categories, keys and approved coverage pass. Every record is accounted for. |
| Category derivation | All 23 categories map exactly once to the approved five groups; counts are preserved and order is chronological. |
| Regression results | For the same checksum-bound input: 15,226 records, 331 authorities and ten final groups; female total **30,420,281**, male **29,177,325**, combined **59,597,606**. All ten age–sex counts match the earlier review. |
| Percentages | Denominators are explicit and positive; unrounded within-sex percentages reconcile within the agreed tolerance. Display rounding is documented. |
| Independent validation | Geography and authoritative benchmark reconciliation are complete; unexplained discrepancies block publication. |
| Failure safety | Adverse fixtures trigger the intended diagnostics and cannot produce a successful published result. |
| Reproducibility | A clean-session run reproduces numerical results using the recorded environment and configuration. |
| Auditability | Source, references, code, configuration, tests, logs and outputs are linked by run ID and retained evidence. |
| Communication and handover | Rendered outputs are accurate and accessible, and another operator can run and troubleshoot the workflow from the documentation. |

The minimum viable solution should therefore be **small but strict**: preserve the valid calculation, make assumptions explicit, and prevent plausible-looking output from being produced when the underlying evidence is incomplete.
