Result: {\"found\":true,\"languageId\":\"r\",\"topic\":\"snapshot\",\"package\":\"renv\",\"content\":\"\\n### Record current state of the project library in the lockfile\\n\\n#### Description\\n\\nCall `renv::snapshot()` to update a lockfile with the current state of\\ndependencies in the project library. The lockfile can be used to later\\nrestore these dependencies as required.\\n\\nIt's also possible to call `renv::snapshot()` with a non-renv project,\\nin which case it will record the current state of dependencies in the\\ncurrent library paths. This makes it possible to restore the current\\npackages, providing lightweight portability and reproducibility without\\nisolation.\\n\\nIf you want to automatically snapshot after each change, you can set\\n`config$config$auto.snapshot(TRUE)` – see `?config` for more details.\\n\\n#### Usage\\n\\n``` R\\nsnapshot(\\n  project = NULL,\\n  ...,\\n  library = NULL,\\n  lockfile = paths$lockfile(project = project),\\n  type = settings$snapshot.type(project = project),\\n  dev = NULL,\\n  repos = getOption(\\\"repos\\\"),\\n  packages = NULL,\\n  exclude = NULL,\\n  prompt = interactive(),\\n  update = FALSE,\\n  force = FALSE,\\n  reprex = FALSE,\\n  description = NULL\\n)\\n```\\n\\n#### Arguments\\n\\n\u003ctable role=\\\"presentation\\\">\\n\u003ccolgroup>\\n\u003ccol style=\\\"width: 50%\\\" />\\n\u003ccol style=\\\"width: 50%\\\" />\\n\u003c/colgroup>\\n\u003ctbody>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"project\\\">project\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>The project directory. If \u003ccode>NULL\u003c/code>, then the active\\nproject will be used. If no project is currently active, then the\\ncurrent working directory is used instead.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"...\\\">...\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>Unused arguments, reserved for future expansion. If any arguments\\nare matched to \u003ccode>...\u003c/code>, renv will signal an error.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"library\\\">library\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>The \u003cspan class=\\\"rlang\\\">\u003cstrong>R\u003c/strong>\u003c/span> libraries to\\nsnapshot. When \u003ccode>NULL\u003c/code>, the active \u003cspan\\nclass=\\\"rlang\\\">\u003cstrong>R\u003c/strong>\u003c/span> libraries (as reported by\\n\u003ccode>.libPaths()\u003c/code>) are used.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"lockfile\\\">lockfile\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>The location where the generated lockfile should be written. By\\ndefault, the lockfile is written to a file called \u003ccode>renv.lock\u003c/code>\\nin the project directory. When \u003ccode>NULL\u003c/code>, the lockfile (as an\\n\u003cspan class=\\\"rlang\\\">\u003cstrong>R\u003c/strong>\u003c/span> object) is returned\\ndirectly instead.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"type\\\">type\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>The type of snapshot to perform:\u003c/p>\\n\u003cul>\\n\u003cli>\u003cp>\u003ccode>\\\"implicit\\\"\u003c/code>, (the default), uses all packages\\ncaptured by \u003ccode>dependencies()\u003c/code>.\u003c/p>\u003c/li>\\n\u003cli>\u003cp>\u003ccode>\\\"explicit\\\"\u003c/code> uses packages recorded in\\n\u003ccode>DESCRIPTION\u003c/code>.\u003c/p>\u003c/li>\\n\u003cli>\u003cp>\u003ccode>\\\"all\\\"\u003c/code> uses all packages in the project\\nlibrary.\u003c/p>\u003c/li>\\n\u003cli>\u003cp>\u003ccode>\\\"custom\\\"\u003c/code> uses a custom filter.\u003c/p>\u003c/li>\\n\u003c/ul>\\n\u003cp>See \u003cstrong>Snapshot types\u003c/strong> below for more details.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"dev\\\">dev\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>Boolean; include development dependencies? These packages are\\ntypically required when developing the project, but not when running it\\n(i.e. you want them installed when humans are working on the project but\\nnot when computers are deploying it).\u003c/p>\\n\u003cp>Development dependencies include packages listed in the\\n\u003ccode>Suggests\u003c/code> field of a \u003ccode>DESCRIPTION\u003c/code> found in the\\nproject root, and roxygen2 or devtools if their use is implied by other\\nproject metadata. They also include packages used in \u003ccode\\nstyle=\\\"white-space: pre;\\\">⁠~/.Rprofile⁠\u003c/code> if\\n\u003ccode>config$user.profile()\u003c/code> is \u003ccode>TRUE\u003c/code>.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"repos\\\">repos\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>The \u003cspan class=\\\"rlang\\\">\u003cstrong>R\u003c/strong>\u003c/span> repositories to\\nbe recorded in the lockfile. Defaults to the currently active package\\nrepositories, as retrieved by \u003ccode>getOption(\\\"repos\\\")\u003c/code>.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"packages\\\">packages\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>A vector of packages to be included in the lockfile. When\\n\u003ccode>NULL\u003c/code> (the default), all packages relevant for the type of\\nsnapshot being performed will be included. When set, the\\n\u003ccode>type\u003c/code> argument is ignored. Recursive dependencies of the\\nspecified packages will be added to the lockfile as well.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"exclude\\\">exclude\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>A vector of packages to be explicitly excluded from the lockfile.\\nNote that transitive package dependencies will always be included, to\\navoid potentially creating an incomplete / non-functional\\nlockfile.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"prompt\\\">prompt\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>Boolean; prompt the user before taking any action? For backwards\\ncompatibility, \u003ccode>confirm\u003c/code> is accepted as an alias for\\n\u003ccode>prompt\u003c/code>.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"update\\\">update\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>Boolean; if the lockfile already exists, then attempt to update\\nthat lockfile without removing any prior package records.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"force\\\">force\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>Boolean; force generation of a lockfile even when pre-flight\\nvalidation checks have failed?\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"reprex\\\">reprex\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>Boolean; generate output appropriate for embedding the lockfile\\nas part of a \u003ca\\nhref=\\\"https://tidyverse.org/help/#reprex\\\">reprex\u003c/a>?\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003ctr>\\n\u003ctd>\u003ccode id=\\\"description\\\">description\u003c/code>\u003c/td>\\n\u003ctd>\u003cp>A package DESCRIPTION, provided either as a named list of\\nDESCRIPTION fields, or a path to a package directory or DESCRIPTION\\nfile. When set, all other arguments are ignored, and a single lockfile\\nrecord for that package is returned.\u003c/p>\u003c/td>\\n\u003c/tr>\\n\u003c/tbody>\\n\u003c/table>\\n\\n#### Value\\n\\nThe generated lockfile, as an \u003cspan class=\\\"rlang\\\">**R**\u003c/span> object\\n(invisibly). Note that this function is normally called for its side\\neffects.\\n\\nWhen `description` is provided, a single lockfile record (a named list)\\nis returned instead.\\n\\n#### Snapshot types\\n\\nDepending on how you prefer to manage your\\n\u003cspan class=\\\"rlang\\\">**R**\u003c/span> package dependencies, you may want to\\nenable an alternate snapshot type.. The types available are as follows:\\n\\n`\\\"implicit\\\"`  \\n(The default) Capture only packages which appear to be used in your\\nproject, as determined by `renv::dependencies()`. This ensures that only\\nthe packages actually required by your project will enter the lockfile;\\nthe downside if it might be slow if your project contains a large number\\nof files. If speed becomes an issue, you might consider using\\n`.renvignore` files to limit which files renv uses for dependency\\ndiscovery, or switching to explicit mode, as described next.\\n\\n`\\\"explicit\\\"`  \\nOnly capture packages which are explicitly listed in the project\\n`DESCRIPTION` file. This workflow is recommended for users who wish to\\nmanage their project's \u003cspan class=\\\"rlang\\\">**R**\u003c/span> package\\ndependencies directly, and can be used for both package and non-package\\n\u003cspan class=\\\"rlang\\\">**R**\u003c/span> projects. Packages used in this manner\\nshould be recorded in either the `Depends` or `Imports` field of the\\n`DESCRIPTION` file.\\n\\n`\\\"all\\\"`  \\nCapture all packages within the active \u003cspan class=\\\"rlang\\\">**R**\u003c/span>\\nlibraries in the lockfile. This is the quickest and simplest method, but\\nmay lead to undesired packages (e.g. development dependencies) entering\\nthe lockfile.\\n\\n`\\\"custom\\\"`  \\nLike `\\\"implicit\\\"`, but use a custom user-defined filter instead. The\\nfilter should be specified by the \u003cspan class=\\\"rlang\\\">**R**\u003c/span>\\noption `renv.snapshot.filter`, and should either be a character vector\\nnaming a function (e.g. `\\\"package::method\\\"`), or be a function itself.\\nThe function should only accept one argument (the project directory),\\nand should return a vector of package names to include in the lockfile.\\n\\nYou can change the snapshot type for the current project with\\n`settings()`. For example, the following code will switch to using\\n`\\\"explicit\\\"` snapshots:\\n\\n    renv::settings$snapshot.type(\\\"explicit\\\")\\n\\nWhen the `packages` argument is set, `type` is ignored, and instead only\\nthe requested set of packages, and their recursive dependencies, will be\\nwritten to the lockfile.\\n\\n#### Package projects\\n\\nWhen snapshotting a package project (that is, a project containing a\\n`DESCRIPTION` file), renv normally records only the package's\\ndependencies in the lockfile, and excludes the package itself. If you'd\\nlike the package itself to be recorded as well – for example, because\\nthe project is deployed as a Shiny application, using an `app.R` that\\nruns an application exported from the package – you can set:\\n\\n    Config/renv/snapshot/include-self: TRUE\\n\\nin the package's `DESCRIPTION` file. With this set, the package is also\\ntreated as a dependency of the project, and so is expected to be\\ninstalled in the project library. Note that for the package to be\\nrestorable, it should be installed from a remote source – for example,\\nwith `renv::install(\\\"\u003cuser>/\u003crepo>\\\")` for a package available on GitHub.\\n\\nThe \u003cspan class=\\\"rlang\\\">**R**\u003c/span> option `renv.snapshot.ignore.self`\\ncan also be used to control this behavior: set it to `FALSE` to include\\nthe package in the lockfile, or `TRUE` to exclude it. When set, this\\noption takes precedence over the `DESCRIPTION` field.\\n\\n#### See Also\\n\\nMore on handling package `dependencies()`\\n\\nOther reproducibility: `lockfiles`, `restore()`\\n\\n#### Examples\\n\\n``` R\\n\\n## Not run: \\n\\n# disable automatic snapshots\\nauto.snapshot \u003c- getOption(\\\"renv.config.auto.snapshot\\\")\\noptions(renv.config.auto.snapshot = FALSE)\\n\\n# initialize a new project (with an empty R library)\\nrenv::init(bare = TRUE)\\n\\n# install digest 0.6.19\\nrenv::install(\\\"digest@0.6.19\\\")\\n\\n# save library state to lockfile\\nrenv::snapshot()\\n\\n# remove digest from library\\nrenv::remove(\\\"digest\\\")\\n\\n# check library status\\nrenv::status()\\n\\n# restore lockfile, thereby reinstalling digest 0.6.19\\nrenv::restore()\\n\\n# restore automatic snapshots\\noptions(renv.config.auto.snapshot = auto.snapshot)\\n\\n\\n## End(Not run)\\n```\"}"},"elapsedMs":2274}</script></tool-result></div>

Result: {\"found\":true,\"languageId\":\"r\",\"topic\":\"rscript...[truncated, total 4135 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"Ran 'positron.help.readHelpTopic'. Result: {\"found\":true,\"languageId\":\"r\",\"topic\":\"rscript\",\"package\":\"callr\",\"content\":\"\\n### Run an R script\\n\\n#### Description\\n\\nIt uses the `Rscript` program corresponding to the current R version, to\\nrun the script. It streams `stdout` and `stderr` of the process.\\n\\n#### Usage\\n\\n``` R\\nrscript(\\n  script,\\n  cmdargs = character(),\\n  libpath = .libPaths(),\\n  repos = default_repos(),\\n  stdout = NULL,\\n  stderr = NULL,\\n  poll_connection = TRUE,\\n  echo = FALSE,\\n  show = TRUE,\\n  callback = NULL,\\n  block_callback = NULL,\\n  spinner = FALSE,\\n  system_profile = FALSE,\\n  user_profile = \\\"project\\\",\\n  env = rcmd_safe_env(),\\n  timeout = Inf,\\n  wd = \\\".\\\",\\n  fail_on_status = TRUE,\\n  color = TRUE,\\n  ...\\n)\\n```\\n\\n#### Arguments\\n\\n|  |  |\\n|----|----|\\n| `script` | Path of the script to run. |\\n| `cmdargs` | Command line arguments. |\\n| `libpath` | The library path. |\\n| `repos` | The `repos` option. If `NULL`, then no `repos` option is set. This options is only used if `user_profile` or `system_profile` is set `FALSE`, as it is set using the system or the user profile. |\\n| `stdout` | Optionally a file name to send the standard output to. |\\n| `stderr` | Optionally a file name to send the standard error to. It may be the same as `stdout`, in which case standard error is redirected to standard output. It can also be the special string `\\\"2>&1\\\"`, in which case standard error will be redirected to standard output. |\\n| `poll_connection` | Whether to have a control connection to the process. This is used to transmit messages from the subprocess to the parent. |\\n| `echo` | Whether to echo the complete command run by `rcmd`. |\\n| `show` | Logical, whether to show the standard output on the screen while the child process is running. Note that this is independent of the `stdout` and `stderr` arguments. The standard error is not shown currently. |\\n| `callback` | A function to call for each line of the standard output and standard error from the child process. It works together with the `show` option; i.e. if `show = TRUE`, and a callback is provided, then the output is shown of the screen, and the callback is also called. |\\n| `block_callback` | A function to call for each block of the standard output and standard error. This callback is not line oriented, i.e. multiple lines or half a line can be passed to the callback. |\\n| `spinner` | Whether to show a calming spinner on the screen while the child R session is running. By default it is shown if `show = TRUE` and the R session is interactive. |\\n| `system_profile` | Whether to use the system profile file. |\\n| `user_profile` | Whether to use the user's profile file. If this is `\\\"project\\\"`, then only the profile from the working directory is used, but the `R_PROFILE_USER` environment variable and the user level profile are not. See also \\\"Security considerations\\\" below. |\\n| `env` | Environment variables to set for the child process. |\\n| `timeout` | Timeout for the function call to finish. It can be a base::difftime object, or a real number, meaning seconds. If the process does not finish before the timeout period expires, then a `system_command_timeout_error` error is thrown. `Inf` means no timeout. |\\n| `wd` | Working directory to use for running the command. Defaults to the current working directory. |\\n| `fail_on_status` | Whether to throw an R error if the command returns with a non-zero status code. By default no error is thrown. |\\n| `color` | Whether to use terminal colors in the child process, assuming they are active in the parent process. |\\n| `...` | Extra arguments are passed to `processx::run()`. |\\n\\n#### Security considerations\\n\\n`callr` makes a copy of the user's `.Renviron` file and potentially of\\nthe local or user `.Rprofile`, in the session temporary directory. Avoid\\nstoring sensitive information such as passwords, in your environment\\nfile or your profile, otherwise this information will get scattered in\\nvarious files, at least temporarily, until the subprocess finishes. Result: {\"found\":true,\"languageId\":\"r\",\"topic\":\"agg_png\",\"package\":\"ragg\",\"content\":\"\\n### Draw to a PNG file\\n\\n#### Description\\n\\nThe PNG (Portable Network Graphic) format is one of the most ubiquitous\\ntoday, due to its versatiliity and widespread support. It supports\\ntransparency as well as both 8 and 16 bit colour. The device uses\\ndefault compression and filtering and will not use a colour palette as\\nthis is less useful for antialiased data. This means that it might be\\npossible to compress the resulting image even more if size is of concern\\n(though the defaults are often very good). In contrast to\\n`grDevices::png()` the date and time will not be written to the file,\\nmeaning that similar plot code will produce identical files (a good\\nfeature if used with version control). It will, however, write in the\\ndimensions of the image based on the `res` argument.\\n\\n#### Usage\\n\\n``` R\\nagg_png(\\n  filename = \\\"Rplot%03d.png\\\",\\n  width = 480,\\n  height = 480,\\n  units = \\\"px\\\",\\n  pointsize = 12,\\n  background = \\\"white\\\",\\n  res = 72,\\n  scaling = 1,\\n  snap_rect = TRUE,\\n  bitsize = 8,\\n  bg\\n)\\n```\\n\\n#### Arguments\\n\\n|  |  |\\n|----|----|\\n| `filename` | The name of the file. Follows the same semantics as the file naming in `grDevices::png()`, meaning that you can provide a `sprintf()` compliant string format to name multiple plots (such as the default value) |\\n| `width`, `height` | The dimensions of the device |\\n| `units` | The unit `width` and `height` is measured in, in either pixels (`'px'`), inches (`'in'`), millimeters (`'mm'`), or centimeter (`'cm'`). |\\n| `pointsize` | The default pointsize of the device in pt. This will in general not have any effect on grid graphics (including ggplot2) as text size is always set explicitly there. |\\n| `background` | The background colour of the device |\\n| `res` | The resolution of the device. This setting will govern how device dimensions given in inches, centimeters, or millimeters will be converted to pixels. Further, it will be used to scale text sizes and linewidths |\\n| `scaling` | A scaling factor to apply to the rendered line width and text size. Useful for getting the right dimensions at the resolution that you need. If e.g. you need to render a plot at 4000x3000 pixels for it to fit into a layout, but you find that the result appears to small, you can increase the `scaling` argument to make everything appear bigger at the same resolution. |\\n| `snap_rect` | Should axis-aligned rectangles drawn with only fill snap to the pixel grid. This will prevent anti-aliasing artifacts when two rectangles are touching at their border. |\\n| `bitsize` | Should the device record colour as 8 or 16bit |\\n| `bg` | Same as `background` for compatibility with old graphic device APIs |\\n\\n#### Examples\\n\\n``` R\\nfile \u003c- tempfile(fileext = '.png')\\nagg_png(file)\\nplot(sin, -pi, 2*pi)\\ndev.off()\\n```\"}"},"elapsedMs":153}</script></tool-result></div>

The safest approach is to preserve **the conversation, the project files and a verified backup** separately. None substitutes for the others.

## 1. Export this conversation

In Posit Assistant’s **gear/overflow menu → Export / Import**, export:

| Format | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **JSON** | Preserves the full conversation-tree structure and supports later import |
| **HTML** | Provides a readable standalone copy and also supports import |
| Markdown, optionally | Convenient for searching and quoting in documentation |

Save **both JSON and HTML**. Open the HTML to check it, and ideally test importing the JSON. Don’t assume an export bundles every source file, image or generated output—preserve those separately.

Conversations are saved automatically, but an independent export is a better backup. Official instructions: https://assistant.posit.co/docs/features/conversations/

## 2. Preserve the project—including the outputs

Make a dated archive of the complete [project folder](.), including the original inputs, R scripts, configuration, reference tables, tests, documentation, [renv.lock](renv.lock) and [outputs/](outputs/).

**Important: your project currently has no Git commits, and its files are untracked.** Also, [`.gitignore`](.gitignore) deliberately excludes generated outputs. A Git backup alone would therefore not currently preserve this work, and even after committing it would omit the run evidence unless handled separately.

I recommend committing the reviewed source, tests and documentation to Git, while preserving the generated outputs in the dated archive. Keep a second copy on a separate drive or backed-up storage location.

## 3. Preserve the handover context

Our existing [implementation notes](docs/implementation_progress.md), [test status](docs/test_status.md) and [deployment instructions](docs/deployment.md) capture much of the context. A short handover summary should also identify the selected run, agreed decisions and outstanding validation questions.

There’s no need to rely on saving the entire R session: the scripts and input data can recreate the results. The saved outputs and manifests preserve evidence of what actually ran.

**My recommendation:** JSON + HTML conversation exports, a dated project archive including outputs, and an initial Git commit—then verify a copy opens correctly. Keep these private until you’ve reviewed them for personal paths or other sensitive information.

<div><tool-result call-id="call_2jnaJnkMCuuvM3MrkoSGgXPl"><script type="application/json">{"version":1,"status":"success","result":{"type":"text","value":"[File: 2.3KB, 39 lines, showing lines 1-39]\n1\t# Methodology and current limits\n2\t\n3\tThis w...[truncated, total 2533 chars]"},"resultPreview":{"type":"code","value":"[File: 2.3KB, 39 lines, showing lines 1-39]\n# Methodology and current limits\n\nThis workflow preserves the reviewed SAS calculation, not its known defects.\nSource counts represent authority–sex–age observations. The original text is\nretained during ingestion; invalid records cause failure, not silent exclusion.\nThe category references are transcriptions of the supplied extract, not externally\nauthenticated ONS codebooks.\n\nAge codes 1–2 map to 0–4, 3–6 to 5–15, 7–9 to 16–24, 10–17 to 25–64,\nand 18–23 to 65+. These are exact unions of source categories. No estimation or\nsplitting of counts is performed. Every mapping must be many-to-one and complete.\n\nCounts are summed across observed authorities within each sex and reporting age\ngroup. A percentage is 100 times the group count divided by the sum across all\nfive groups for the same sex. The machine-readable result retains the denominator\nand full-precision percentage. Round to one decimal place only when displaying;\nthe rounded male percentages total 100.1%, which is an expected rounding effect.\n\nThe supplied-file regression expectations are female 30,420,281, male 29,177,325\nand combined 59,597,606. All ten reviewed group counts are in\n`tests/expected/ons_rm121_2021_results.csv`. These expectations are tied to the\nsource checksum in the tests. They are not independently verified official totals.\n\nCSV and PNG outputs are explicitly provisional and remain inside a run-specific\n`review/` directory. The count chart uses separate sex panels with a shared\nscale, so colour is not needed to identify sex. The age groups have unequal widths\nand 65+ is open-ended; the bars are totals, not densities or counts per year of age.\n\nGeography coverage is checked only within observed authorities. No authoritative\ngeography list or comparable official benchmark has been supplied, so independent\ncoverage and official acceptance remain blocked. The geographical scope and year\nare descriptions inherited from the supplied files, not external certification.\nThe workflow cannot promote itself to official acceptance by editing a status flag.\n\nFuture adapters must validate their own source schemas and domains. Exact mappings\nmust respect classification boundaries. Source and grouping keys must retain\nperiods and other context that define separate populations. Do not sum snapshots,\noverlapping geography levels, incompatible classifications, rates or percentages.\n"},"elapsedMs":7}</script></tool-result></div>

Use it to look a package up rather than\nscanning the whole list, and to answer \"is X installed?\" reliably.\n\n**Reading the payload:**\n\n- `packages` holds the named packages that **are** installed, with full detail.\n- `notFound` holds the names that are **not** installed. A name here is a\n  definitive \"not installed\" -- that is the reason to name packages rather than\n  to search the compact list, which can be large.\n- `metadataStatus` and `vulnerabilityStatus` mean the same as elsewhere (see\n  above and the advisories section below).\n- The same `available: false` reasons apply. In addition, if you call it\n  without any names it returns `reason: 'no-names'` -- pass the package names.\n\n**Arguments:**\n- `names` (array of string): The package names to look up, as the package repository knows them (for example: dplyr, pandas). Pass an array of names, or a single name. Matching is case-insensitive.\n\n**Returns:** An object with available: true, the session the packages belong to, packages (the named packages that are installed, with full detail), notFound (the named packages that are not installed -- a name here is a definitive \"not installed\", not a truncated-away answer), metadataStatus (how the outdated state was obtained: 'fresh', 'cached', 'unsupported', 'timed-out', or 'fetch-failed'), and vulnerabilityStatus (how advisories were obtained). Each installed package carries name, version, latestVersion, outdated, attached, description, url, license, author, sourceRepository, publishedDate, title, and vulnerabilities. vulnerabilities are the security advisories against the installed version, worst first (id, osvId, score, scoreVersion, severity of 'critical'/'high'/'medium'/'low'/'unscored', summary, fixedIn, published, url); an empty array means the repository was asked and reports nothing against that version, which is an all-clear, while an absent field means there is no advisory data for that package at all, which is not. vulnerabilityStatus says how the advisories were obtained: 'fresh' (Package Manager queried now), 'cached' (the cached advisories were still current), 'disabled' (advisory lookups are turned off in settings), 'unavailable' (a lookup ran and produced nothing, which is not worth retrying), or 'timed-out' (the lookup ran out of time partway). vulnerabilitySource names the Package Manager host that served them and when it answered. When no packages are named, an object with available: false and reason 'no-names'. When there are no packages to report at all, an object with available: false and a reason of 'disabled', 'no-session', 'session-not-ready', 'unsupported', or 'failed' -- the last of which also carries a message.\n"},"elapsedMs":9}</script></tool-result></div>

Result: {\"found\":true,\"languageId\":\"r\",\"topic\":\"zipr\",\"package\":\"zip\",\"content\":\"\\n### Compress Files into 'zip' Archives\\n\\n#### Description\\n\\n`zip()` creates a new zip archive file.\\n\\n#### Usage\\n\\n``` R\\nzip(\\n  zipfile,\\n  files,\\n  recurse = TRUE,\\n  compression_level = 9,\\n  include_directories = TRUE,\\n  root = \\\".\\\",\\n  mode = c(\\\"mirror\\\", \\\"cherry-pick\\\")\\n)\\n\\nzipr(\\n  zipfile,\\n  files,\\n  recurse = TRUE,\\n  compression_level = 9,\\n  include_directories = TRUE,\\n  root = \\\".\\\",\\n  mode = c(\\\"cherry-pick\\\", \\\"mirror\\\")\\n)\\n\\nzip_append(\\n  zipfile,\\n  files,\\n  recurse = TRUE,\\n  compression_level = 9,\\n  include_directories = TRUE,\\n  root = \\\".\\\",\\n  mode = c(\\\"mirror\\\", \\\"cherry-pick\\\")\\n)\\n\\nzipr_append(\\n  zipfile,\\n  files,\\n  recurse = TRUE,\\n  compression_level = 9,\\n  include_directories = TRUE,\\n  root = \\\".\\\",\\n  mode = c(\\\"cherry-pick\\\", \\\"mirror\\\")\\n)\\n```\\n\\n#### Arguments\\n\\n|  |  |\\n|----|----|\\n| `zipfile` | The zip file to create. If the file exists, `zip` overwrites it, but `zip_append` appends to it. If it is a directory an error is thrown. |\\n| `files` | List of file to add to the archive. See details below about absolute and relative path names. |\\n| `recurse` | Whether to add the contents of directories recursively. |\\n| `compression_level` | A number between 1 and 9. 9 compresses best, but it also takes the longest. |\\n| `include_directories` | Whether to explicitly include directories in the archive. Including directories might confuse MS Office when reading docx files, so set this to `FALSE` for creating them. |\\n| `root` | Change to this working directory before creating the archive. |\\n| `mode` | Selects how files and directories are stored in the archive. It can be `\\\"mirror\\\"` or `\\\"cherry-pick\\\"`. See \\\"Relative Paths\\\" below for details. |\\n\\n#### Details\\n\\n`zip_append()` appends compressed files to an existing 'zip' file.\\n\\n##### Relative paths\\n\\n`zip()` and `zip_append()` can run in two different modes: mirror mode\\nand cherry picking mode. They handle the specified `files` differently.\\n\\n###### Mirror mode\\n\\nMirror mode is for creating the zip archive of a directory structure,\\nexactly as it is on the disk. The current working directory will be the\\nroot of the archive, and the paths will be fully kept. zip changes the\\ncurrent directory to `root` before creating the archive.\\n\\nE.g. consider the following directory structure:\\n\\n    .\\n    |-- foo\\n    |   |-- bar\\n    |   |   |-- file1\\n    |   |   `-- file2\\n    |   `-- bar2\\n    `-- foo2\\n        `-- file3\\n\\nAssuming the current working directory is `foo`, the following zip\\nentries are created by `zip`:\\n\\n    setwd(\\\"foo\\\")\\n    zip::zip(\\\"../test.zip\\\", c(\\\"bar/file1\\\", \\\"bar2\\\", \\\"../foo2\\\"))\\n    #> Warning in warn_for_dotdot(data$key): Some paths reference parent directory,\\n    #> creating non-portable zip file\\n    zip_list(\\\"../test.zip\\\")[, \\\"filename\\\", drop = FALSE]\\n    #> # A data frame: 4 x 1\\n    #>   filename     \\n    #>   \u003cchr>        \\n    #> 1 bar/file1    \\n    #> 2 bar2/        \\n    #> 3 ../foo2/     \\n    #> 4 ../foo2/file3\\n\\nNote that zip refuses to store files with absolute paths, and chops off\\nthe leading `/` character from these file names. This is because only\\nrelative paths are allowed in zip files.\\n\\n###### Cherry picking mode\\n\\nIn cherry picking mode, the selected files and directories will be at\\nthe root of the archive. This mode is handy if you want to select a\\nsubset of files and directories, possibly from different paths and put\\nall of the in the archive, at the top level.\\n\\nHere is an example with the same directory structure as above:\\n\\n    zip::zip(\\n      \\\"../test2.zip\\\",\\n      c(\\\"bar/file1\\\", \\\"bar2\\\", \\\"../foo2\\\"),\\n      mode = \\\"cherry-pick\\\"\\n    )\\n    zip_list(\\\"../test2.zip\\\")[, \\\"filename\\\", drop = FALSE]\\n    #> # A data frame: 4 x 1\\n    #>   filename  \\n    #>   \u003cchr>     \\n    #> 1 file1     \\n    #> 2 bar2/     \\n    #> 3 foo2/     \\n    #> 4 foo2/file3\\n\\nFrom zip version 2.3.0, `\\\".\\\"` has a special meaning in the `files`\\nargument: it will include the files (and possibly directories) within\\nthe current working directory, but **not** the working directory itself.\\nNote that this only applies to cherry picking mode.\\n\\n##### Permissions:\\n\\n`zip()` (and `zip_append()`, etc.) add the permissions of the archived\\nfiles and directories to the ZIP archive, on Unix systems. Most zip and\\nunzip implementations support these, so they will be recovered after\\nextracting the archive.\\n\\nNote, however that the owner and group (uid and gid) are currently\\nomitted, even on Unix.\\n\\n##### `zipr()` and `zipr_append()`\\n\\nThese function exist for historical reasons. They are identical to\\n`zip()` and `zipr_append()` with a different default for the `mode`\\nargument.\\n\\n#### Value\\n\\nThe name of the created zip file, invisibly.\\n\\n#### Examples\\n\\n``` R\\n## Some files to zip up. We will run all this in the R session's\\n## temporary directory, to avoid messing up the user's workspace.\\ndir.create(tmp \u003c- tempfile())\\ndir.create(file.path(tmp, \\\"mydir\\\"))\\ncat(\\\"first file\\\", file = file.path(tmp, \\\"mydir\\\", \\\"file1\\\"))\\ncat(\\\"second file\\\", file = file.path(tmp, \\\"mydir\\\", \\\"file2\\\"))\\n\\nzipfile \u003c- tempfile(fileext = \\\".zip\\\")\\nzip::zip(zipfile, \\\"mydir\\\", root = tmp)\\n\\n## List contents\\nzip_list(zipfile)\\n\\n## Add another file\\ncat(\\\"third file\\\", file = file.path(tmp, \\\"mydir\\\", \\\"file3\\\"))\\nzip_append(zipfile, file.path(\\\"mydir\\\", \\\"file3\\\"), root = tmp)\\nzip_list(zipfile)\\n```\"}"},"elapsedMs":404}</script></tool-result></div>

## Then: the first Git commit

After reviewing the exports, we’ll stage only the intended project files—not use `git add .`—inspect the staged selection, and make the first commit. Outputs and ZIP bundles will remain outside Git because they are preserved separately.

Finally, copy the complete bundle folder to another drive or protected backup location. The copy inside this project is a snapshot, **not yet an off-machine backup**.
